questions.question: Why does vector search struggle with 'Who should I page if a checkout dependency breaks?'
options: The answer is a chain of facts, and the later links ('Mina Shah leads the warehouse team') don't resemble the question
questions.explanation: Similarity finds text that looks like the question; a graph finds text connected to it.

questions.question: Why is each triple indexed under both of its nodes?
options: So walks go in both directions: from a service you can reach the team that owns it
questions.explanation: Questions often need edges in the reverse direction from how they were written.

questions.question: How many hops did the paging question need to get all six facts, and what did that cost?
options: Three hops, 12 lines: almost the whole graph, including irrelevant teams
questions.explanation: Each hop adds every neighbour of every node reached; filtering relations keeps it manageable.

questions.question: 'The payments team meets on Tuesdays' produced no triple. What does this illustrate?
options: Extraction loses information that fits no relation, so keep source ids to get back to the original text
questions.explanation: A graph is a lossy view of the text.

questions.question: When is graph retrieval worth the cost of building the graph?
options: When important questions follow chains of relations (ownership, dependencies, reporting lines) that similarity search misses
questions.explanation: For one-hop questions it added nothing in this lesson.
